title: The Incumbents Are Coming | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z partner Seema Amble argues that enterprise systems of record (Salesforce, Docusign, Atlassian, Jira) are climbing an agent hierarchy from retrieval to policy-level judgment, while general agents like Claude sit above them as the front door — the Claudeforce partnership being the template. Her contrarian carve-out: incumbents' learning stays bounded by the record they own, so vertical AI-native startups can win by manufacturing a training curriculum (as Harvey did with ~1,750 legal-task environments) and owning the cross-system job itself.

insights.claim: Enterprise systems of record become more valuable, not less, as AI agents proliferate, because the data and actions those systems control are what agents must operate on to get work done.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Cuts against the 'AI kills SaaS seats' short thesis — incumbent record-owners retain a toll position on agentic workflows.
insights.quote: The bullish case for incumbent systems of record is that AI makes systems of record get more important, not less.
insights.locator: The bullish case for incumbent systems

insights.claim: Salesforce and Anthropic's Claudeforce lets a user work with the Salesforce CRM from inside Claude without opening Salesforce, making a general-purpose agent the front door while Salesforce keeps the underlying CRM data and actions.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: The template deal for how labs and incumbents split the stack — watch whether interface value or record value accrues the pricing power.
insights.quote: Claudeforce lets you work with the Salesforce CRM from inside Claude without having to open Salesforce (or so they claim!).
insights.locator: This is what Salesforce just announced

insights.claim: Incumbents are shipping products that take action rather than just store information: Docusign's Iris reviews contracts, Atlassian's Rovo resolves and routes requests, and Klaviyo's Composer builds campaigns and assesses marketing performance.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Named evidence that the 'slap on a chatbot' phase is over; these products are the direct competitive set for point-solution AI startups.
insights.quote: These products move incumbents beyond the “slap on a chatbot” strategy and into taking action.
insights.locator: Docusign’s Iris reviews contracts

insights.claim: Incumbents have a direct commercial incentive to control and charge for access to their data while simultaneously pushing their own agents forward, so data-access pricing becomes a competitive weapon rather than a neutral integration decision.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: API/data-egress terms are the chokepoint to monitor for any AI startup dependent on incumbent connectors.
insights.locator: The incumbents have an incentive to control

insights.claim: The interface layer and the system of record are unbundling as general agents coordinate work across applications, which creates the specific opening for AI-native startups to rebundle around the job rather than around the data store.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Frames the whole app-layer investment question: back rebundlers of jobs, not builders of another record.
insights.quote: The interface and the system of record look like they’re unbundling, creating an opening for AI-native startups to rebundle around the job.
insights.locator: At the same time, Claude is starting to coordinate

insights.claim: Application-level agents can be sorted into four tiers by how much autonomy and judgment they require: retrieval assistants (find, summarize, draft), process agents (rule-based record updates and routing), policy agents (apply playbooks, precedents and thresholds to ambiguous cases), and principal agents (open-ended judgment on strategy, risk and resources).
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: A diligence rubric: ask which tier a company's product actually operates at, since price and defensibility rise with judgment.
insights.locator: The agent hierarchy

insights.claim: A year ago most incumbents' AI products were still at the retrieval stage functioning as chatbots and analytical tools, and only now can more of them take action using the workflows, permissions and rules already embedded in their products.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Sets the clock on incumbent catch-up speed — roughly one tier per year is the observed pace to underwrite against.
insights.quote: A year ago, most incumbents’ AI products were still at the retrieval stage, if that.
insights.locator: A year ago, most incumbents’ AI products

insights.claim: Judgment-level agent capability breaks down precisely when a decision depends on information outside the record the incumbent manages, which is why incumbent policy agents like Docusign's Iris remain bounded by their own data.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: The testable boundary of incumbent encroachment — startups should target jobs whose decisive inputs sit outside any one record.
insights.quote: Judgment gets harder when the decision depends on information outside the record that the incumbent manages.
insights.locator: A few are beginning to apply narrow, human-defined policy

themes.theme: The job is bigger than the record

insights.claim: The customer's job to be done is structurally larger than any single record — the contract is not the legal matter, the ticket is not the customer's resolution, and the opportunity is not the sale — so a record owner can only build a 'local system of work'.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: The sharpest test for whether an incumbent can actually absorb a startup's category: does the job stay inside one record?
insights.quote: The contract is not the legal matter, the ticket is not the customer’s resolution, and the opportunity is not the sale.
insights.locator: A customer’s work gets done through a combination

insights.claim: The incumbent's limit is not a hard technical boundary since they can pull in outside data and add workflows, but their work always expands outward from the record they already own, giving them a directional handicap rather than a wall.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Tempering the moat story — incumbent limits are gravitational, not absolute, so startup leads are timing advantages that must be spent.
insights.quote: This isn’t a hard technical boundary because incumbents can pull in outside data and add workflows, but their work still expands outward from the record they already own.
insights.locator: The job is bigger than the record

insights.claim: General-purpose agents suffer concrete mechanical frictions when reaching across systems: even using MCP, pulling information across applications has latency, and each application may describe the same customer, contract or transaction differently.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Latency and schema mismatch are the measurable reasons cross-app general agents underperform — verify these are actually solved before writing off vertical tools.
insights.quote: Even using MCP, pulling info across applications has latency, and each application may describe the same customer, contract, or transaction differently.
insights.locator: A general purpose agent like Claude or Codex

insights.claim: Even an agent with access to every application inside one company does not automatically get information held by external parties such as between buyers and suppliers, making multi-party jobs the hardest terrain for a general agent to occupy.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Favors startups whose product spans company boundaries — cross-org network position is the least replicable asset here.
insights.locator: Even if a general purpose agent can access every app

insights.claim: Claude can keep gaining context through deeper integrations blessed by the incumbents, meaning the general agent's reach is partly a function of incumbent cooperation rather than pure technical capability.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Watch the pace of incumbent-blessed integrations as the leading indicator of how much surface the labs take from the app layer.
insights.locator: And Claude can keep gaining context

insights.claim: Completed records do not automatically suffice as a training curriculum, because a signed contract shows what parties agreed to but not the alternatives considered or reasons for exceptions, and a closed ticket shows the resolution but not the hypotheses the support team tested.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Directly devalues the 'we sit on 20 years of customer data' pitch — historical records lack the decision trace that actually trains judgment.
insights.quote: Completed records alone don’t automatically suffice as a training curriculum for the work.
insights.locator: How vertical AI learns

insights.claim: Because the frontier labs are building general-purpose memory, merely preserving customer context is not a durable competitive advantage for an application company.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Deflates 'context moat' claims in app-layer pitches — memory features get commoditized by the model layer.
insights.quote: The labs are also building general-purpose memory, so preserving context alone is not a durable advantage.
insights.locator: Remembering vs. learning

insights.claim: Remembering and learning are different capabilities: memory lets an agent recall a preference or last week's decision, but it cannot tell the agent whether the work was good, why an expert changed it, or what to change next time.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: A one-question diligence filter: does the product capture expert corrections and outcomes, or just conversation history?
insights.quote: But it doesn’t tell the agent whether the work was good or why an expert changed it or what to change next time.
insights.locator: Memory can help a general purpose agent recall

insights.claim: The unit that improves is the system — model plus vertical harness of context, tools, workflows and evals — using the agent's work, expert feedback and outcomes to improve the next attempt, not the model alone.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Reframes where app-layer value accrues: harness and eval assets, which do not get eaten by the next model release.
insights.quote: A model performs better on a specific job via a vertical harness with the right context, tools, workflows and evals.
insights.locator: How vertical AI learns

insights.claim: Vertical focus compounds by letting a company see more examples of the same job, learn faster, and get better at measuring improvement — measurement quality itself being part of the advantage.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Narrow-then-expand beats broad-then-deepen; a startup's eval sophistication is a proxy for durable lead.
insights.locator: Focus lets the company see more examples

insights.claim: There are two distinct kinds of learning to capture — the profession (how a good professional does the work) and the institution (a firm's templates, precedents, risk thresholds and escalation rules) — and lessons about the profession improve the product for every customer while lessons about one firm may only improve it for that firm.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Separates the scalable asset from the per-account asset — profession-level learning is what actually creates multi-tenant margin.
insights.locator: Profession and Institution

insights.claim: Long-running agents that work over hours or days through complex logic chains with many intermediate decisions and handoffs depend disproportionately on learning-loop quality, and the longer-horizon task can be unbundled and evaluated through a set of checkpoints.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Checkpoint-level evaluation is the operational answer to long-horizon agent reliability — a concrete thing to ask companies to demo.
insights.locator: Long running agents especially benefit

insights.claim: Incumbents will also learn from work performed inside their products, but that learning covers only their slice of the job — contract review inside Docusign, ticket resolution inside Jira, or pipeline updates inside Salesforce.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Incumbent data flywheels are real but partial — the gap between the slice and the whole job is the startup's addressable wedge.
insights.locator: To be clear, incumbents will also learn

insights.claim: As open-weight models and post-training increase, assembling the right data and evals becomes more important than raw model access, shifting differentiation from model choice to curriculum construction.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Model commoditization argues for valuing proprietary eval/curriculum assets over closed-model partnerships.
insights.quote: As open-weight models and post-training increase, assembling the right data and evals becomes even more important.
insights.locator: To learn both the profession and the institution

insights.claim: Harvey post-trained an open-weight model for its Tenet work using synthetic data, public legal data and human-expert-created data, without using customer data to start.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Proof that cold-start data disadvantage is surmountable — undercuts the incumbent-data-moat objection in legal and adjacent verticals.
insights.locator: How Harvey manufactured the curriculum

insights.claim: Harvey created roughly 1,750 legal-task environments, each simulating a partner-assigned matter complete with documents, tools and an expert rubric, with the average assignment carrying about 50 specific grading criteria.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark of what a credible manufactured curriculum costs — use ~1,750 environments x ~50 criteria as the yardstick for rival claims.
insights.quote: It created roughly 1,750 legal-task environments, each simulating a partner-assigned matter, complete with documents and tools and an expert rubric for a high-quality result.
insights.locator: How Harvey manufactured the curriculum

insights.claim: A vertical startup can manufacture a curriculum for the profession first and then use production usage to learn the institution, so it does not need to begin with the largest stock of historical data.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Changes the sequencing of go-to-market: buy or build expert-authored environments before chasing data-rich logos.
insights.locator: To learn both the profession and the institution

insights.claim: The startup's endgame is taking responsibility for the result itself, which requires solving practical frictions around data rights, systems and permissioning and fitting into daily work — deployment and responsibility being the decisive variables.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Points to outcome-based pricing and liability-bearing models as the monetization endpoint for vertical AI.
insights.quote: Deployment and responsibility are key here!
insights.locator: The startup’s opportunity is to put it all together

insights.claim: A four-part test scores vertical AI markets: can an expert quickly tell what the AI got right or wrong and explain how to improve it; is the work hard enough that judgment matters versus simple rules; does the work happen often enough for the product to learn; and can the startup begin with one assignment and grow into an entire job.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: A ready-made screen for deal flow — markets failing any leg lack the learning loop that makes vertical AI defensible.
insights.locator: What makes a good vertical AI market?

insights.claim: Legal, tax and accounting workflows pass the vertical AI test because the work repeats, requires judgment, and experts already review the results as part of normal practice.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Existing expert review infrastructure is a free labeling pipeline — prioritize verticals where it already exists.
insights.locator: Many workflows in legal, tax, and accounting

insights.claim: Industrial manufacturing quality investigation is a non-obvious market fitting the same pattern: when a defect appears, a quality engineer must gather test results, supplier documents, equipment logs and plant rules across several systems, and while one incumbent may store the defect report, no single product owns the full investigation.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: An underpriced hunting ground versus crowded legal AI — screen industrial workflows where the record is fragmented across suppliers and plant systems.
insights.locator: This pattern also shows up in less obvious markets

insights.claim: The winning entry motion is to start with one piece of a job such as drafting the investigation report and expand over time to own the end-to-end resolution, learning both how a good practitioner works and how a specific plant, customer or auditor does it.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: Land-and-expand at the job level, not the seat level, is the pattern to underwrite in early-stage vertical AI.
insights.locator: A startup could begin with one piece of this work

insights.claim: There are jobs where a system of record plus a general-purpose agent will simply be enough, so the vertical AI opportunity is conditional rather than universal and concentrates where work is frequent, judgment matters, and the learning loop is strong.
insights.speaker: Seema Amble
insights.so_what: An explicit concession that limits the addressable set — apply the frequency/judgment/loop filter before funding another vertical agent.
insights.quote: The incumbent may own the record and the lab may control the front door, but the vertical AI company can still win by becoming the best at doing the job itself.
insights.locator: The job is still up for grabs
